summary: Defines guidance for a SIP user agent to create anonymous messages itself, using mechanisms such as GRUUs and TURN, so it does not need a privacy service from RFC 3323. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking a helper to hide your name on a letter, this explains how to hide it yourself using tools your own device already has.

questions: how can a sip user agent be anonymous
how can a sip phone be anonymous
what is a gruu in sip
subtitle: How a SIP phone can hide its user's identity without needing a privacy service.

tldr.problem: RFC 3323 defined SIP privacy using an external privacy service that strips identifying information from messages. New SIP features (GRUU and TURN) let a phone do this itself.
tldr.mechanism: A user agent requests a temporary Globally Routable User Agent URI (GRUU) from its SIP server to anonymize its contact address, and obtains a relay IP address from a TURN server to hide its real network location. The phone then makes calls using these anonymous addresses.
tldr.outcome: A SIP user agent can now withhold its own identity using extensions that were not available in 2002, giving it more control over privacy without depending on a separate network service.

facts.label: Required for anonymity
facts.value: Temporary GRUU and TURN IP address

facts.label: Domain name visibility
facts.value: Always visible in Contact header via GRUU

facts.label: SIP-Identity compatibility
facts.value: Requires domain name in From header; breaks sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid approach

today: RFC 5767 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It describes user-agent-driven privacy for SIP, and implementations supporting GRUU and TURN can follow this guidance. However, many SIP deployments do not require client-side privacy and use RFC 3323 privacy services when needed. The RFC is most relevant for privacy-conscious SIP implementers and for networks where client-side privacy is a design requirement.

sections.title: Privacy Without a Privacy Service
sections.content:
RFC 3323 defined SIP privacy by routing calls through a separate privacy service that removed identifying information from messages before forwarding them. This worked, but required infrastructure outside the user agent itself. Since 2002, new SIP extensions have emerged that let a user agent (UA) handle privacy directly: GRUU (Globally Routable User Agent URIs, RFC 5627) allows a UA to obtain an anonymous contact address from its registrar, and TURN (Traversal Using Relays Around NAT, RFC 5766) lets it obtain an IP address from a relay server. RFC 5767 explains how a UA can combine these to create anonymous SIP messages without needing an external privacy service.

This approach does not obsolete RFC 3323 entirely. When a SIP request carries a P-Asserted-Identity header (used in trusted networks to assert the caller's real identity), the RFC 3323 privacy service may still be needed to prevent that header from leaking outside the trust domain. But for user-controlled anonymity, a UA can now act independently.
sections.plainLanguage: New tools let your phone hide its own identity. You do not need a helper on the network anymore.

sections.title: Getting Anonymous Addresses: GRUU and TURN
sections.content:
The Contact header of a SIP request or response tells the other party where to send future messages. Without privacy, this header reveals the user's device address. A UA wanting anonymity must obtain a temporary GRUU (temp-gruu) by sending a REGISTER request asking for it. If the SIP registrar supports GRUU, it responds with a temporary URI that is functional—other UAs can route calls to it—but does not identify the user or device. The UA then uses this temporary GRUU in its Contact header for all dialog-forming requests and mid-dialog requests.

IP addresses can also reveal identity. The Via header in a SIP request lists the IP address and port where the sender is listening for responses. The SDP body in a SIP INVITE can include the sender's IP address for media. To hide these, a UA must obtain an anonymous IP address from a STUN relay server (TURN). The UA sends media and signals through the relay, so only the relay's IP appears in Via and SDP. The RFC assumes a UA is configured with one or more TURN server addresses, either manually or through a configuration framework.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask your phone company for a fake address to use instead of your real address, and you ask a relay for a fake IP so your phone's location is hidden.

sections.title: What Information Is Critical to Hide
sections.content:
Not all privacy-sensitive information is equally critical. The From header in a SIP request contains the caller's identity (display name and SIP URI). For anonymity, the UA must set this to "Anonymous" and either use "sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid" (which hides the domain but breaks SIP-Identity signing) or use "sip:anonymous@real.domain" (which reveals the domain but allows SIP-Identity). The RFC recommends the first approach for true anonymity, but acknowledges the trade-off.

Optional headers like Subject, User-Agent, and Call-Info can leak identity. A UA should omit these or set them to generic values. The hostname in a Call-ID header can reveal a device; a UA should hide or randomize it. However, GRUU necessarily reveals the domain name in the Contact header—if that domain is small or unique, the caller's affiliation may still be guessed. For complete anonymity, the RFC suggests using a third-party anonymization service outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Hide your name and your device address. Some headers are less critical, but a domain name always leaks which company you work for.

sections.title: Building and Sending an Anonymous SIP Message
sections.content:
A UA compliant with RFC 5767 must follow these steps when privacy is requested. First, anonymize the Contact header using a temp-GRUU if available; otherwise, omit the Contact header or use a generic value. Second, anonymize the From header by setting the display-name to "Anonymous" and the URI to either sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid (true anonymity) or sip:anonymous@yourdom.com (SIP-Identity compatible). Third, anonymize the Via header by obtaining an anonymous IP from a TURN relay and placing that IP in the Via header; route the request to the TURN relay itself so the relay sees the request and routes it onward. Fourth, anonymize IP addresses in SDP by using the anonymous TURN-derived address for media.

Additionally, the UA should conceal hostnames in Call-ID, Warning, and other optional headers. It must not include information identifying the user in optional headers such as Subject, User-Agent, Server, Organization, or Referred-By. When using a relay, the UA must send requests through the relay to ensure request and response follow the same path, maintaining the appearance of anonymity.
sections.plainLanguage: When making a call, use the fake address in all the places your real address would appear. Route the call through a relay so the network cannot see where it came from.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Limitations
sections.content:
True anonymity via GRUU always leaks the domain name, since GRUU requires a valid domain for routing to work. If a receiver knows the caller's company or organization, the domain alone may be enough to identify them. A compromised registrar or TURN server can reveal the caller's identity to the service provider. If many users share a GRUU registrar, the temporary GRUU provides no confidentiality against peers authorized to obtain temporary GRUUs for the same address of record.

The RFC emphasizes that RFC 5767 offers privacy from the remote party, not from intermediate network equipment or malicious insiders. For users who need strong anonymity, a third-party anonymization service—a registrar and TURN provider with no affiliation to the caller's regular provider—is suggested. This is outside the scope of the RFC, but it is the only way to achieve anonymity that even the caller's own SIP server provider cannot penetrate. The RFC recommends that users concerned with privacy consult their provider or seek such a third-party service.
sections.plainLanguage: Your company's domain name is always visible, so people still know who you work for. A real privacy expert would use a service completely separate from your company.
